name: Aaron Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A hundred and ten acres of apples and pears, with sheep grazing under the old trees and a bit of hay off the top fields. November is pruning season, so I'm out at half seven with the loppers and a flask, working down the rows with my two men, cutting out the wood that won't fruit next year. The rest of the time I'm in the cold store checking the fruit, because a pear that's kept a day too long goes from perfect to mush.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love grafting. You take a cutting from an old variety and join it to a young root, and if you've done it right, you've got a tree that'll outlive you. I've grafted trees my grandchildren will pick from. What wears me out is September, when the fruit is ready all at once and I'm short of pickers and praying it doesn't hail.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's with you on the farm and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Teresa does the farm-gate shop and the juice, and she runs the Sunday school. Two full-time men, Rui and Glyn, and about twenty-five pickers in September. Our son Matthew flies for an airline, and our daughter Clare is a pharmacist in town.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, and I'm not ashamed of it. I photograph a branch and it tells me if it's canker or just frost damage. It helps me plan spraying around the weather. I've got it reading the cold store sensors too. Teresa says I talk to my phone more than I talk to her, which is unfair, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a fine tool and every grower should be using it. At the fruit growers' association I'm the one telling them to try it. Some of the older lads think I've gone soft in the head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it stays a tool, I'm a bit ahead and that's all. Good for me, no harm to anyone. I'd have liked more, honestly. I'd like it to tell me when to pick to the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spend about six thousand on more sensors in the orchard, for frost and soil moisture. Try one of the new picking platforms, which are trailers the pickers stand on instead of ladders. Keep Rui and Glyn as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe. I like a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of the older lads think you've gone soft. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My grandfather was the first in the valley to use a tractor sprayer and they laughed at him too. Then they all bought one. It's the same story every generation, just a different machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Teresa think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm a boy with a new toy. She's right, partly. But she was the one who told me to photograph the canker, because she was tired of me ringing the adviser on a Sunday.

S0.say: It's a fine tool, and every grower should be using it. At the fruit growers' association I'm the one telling them to try it, and some older lads think I've gone soft.
S0.think: If it stays a tool, I'm a bit ahead and that's all, good for me and no harm to anyone. I'd have liked more, like telling me the exact day to pick.
S0.do: Spends about six thousand on frost and soil moisture sensors in the orchard and tries a picking platform trailer instead of ladders. Keeps his two workers, Rui and Glyn, as they are.
S0.feel: Calm and a little restless, since he likes a project.
S0.quote: My grandfather was the first in the valley to use a tractor sprayer and they laughed at him too. Then they all bought one.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is energetic and sees himself in a family line of early adopters. His love of grafting shows he thinks in decades. He takes ribbing from older growers lightly and enjoys being ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is a shame, I'd rather it came faster. But fewer jobs for young people is serious. Firms should take on apprentices, and families and churches should help young folk find a trade. That's better than any government scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, slow means I get to stay ahead longer, which is fine. What bothers me is that I can't find young people who want to learn pruning and grafting already. If firms hire even fewer, maybe some of them will come to me. That's the strange upside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take on one apprentice for two years, around eighteen thousand a year, and teach them pruning, grafting and the tech side. Put a notice up at church and the agricultural college. Buy the frost prediction system that's been tested on two farms in the association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit hopeful. If it means one more young person learns to graft, I'm happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does it matter so much that someone learns to graft?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when I go, the old varieties in my orchard go with me if nobody knows how to keep them. I've got a russet that my grandfather brought from his father's farm. You can't buy it anywhere. If nobody grafts it, it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour families and churches over government. Would you accept a government apprenticeship grant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. I'm not daft. If they're paying firms to train people, that's money going into work, not into sitting at home. I'd fill the form in that afternoon, using AI probably.

S1.say: Slow is a shame and I'd rather it came faster. Fewer jobs for young people is serious, and firms, families and churches should help young folk into a trade before any government scheme.
S1.think: Slow means I stay ahead longer, which is fine. I already can't find young people who want to learn pruning and grafting, so if firms hire fewer, maybe some will come to me.
S1.do: Takes on an apprentice for two years at around eighteen thousand a year to learn pruning, grafting and the technology. Advertises at church and the agricultural college, and buys a frost prediction system proven on two association farms.
S1.feel: Calm and a little hopeful, especially if it means another young person learns to graft.
S1.quote: I've got a russet that my grandfather brought from his father's farm. You can't buy it anywhere. If nobody grafts it, it's gone.
S1.fieldNote: He finds an upside where others see a threat: young people might turn to trades like his. His real fear is losing old apple varieties, not jobs. He's pragmatic about government money if it's tied to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on the office workers, and I'm sorry for them, but the economy has always changed and people have always found new work. I'd want the politicians to stop shouting and get out of the way. Help people retrain, but don't stop progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. I'd use one of those assistants for the farm office, the export paperwork, the spraying records. It would save me ten hours a week, which I'd spend in the orchard. I'd feel a bit sorry for the man at the fruit co-op who does our paperwork now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up an assistant for the farm office in the first two months. Use the saved time to start a juice and cider line properly, with Teresa running it, maybe twenty thousand on a small press and bottler. Ask the co-op if they need help using the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pleased, mostly. Guilty about the co-op man, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the co-op man?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Philip. He's done our paperwork for twenty years. He sends Teresa a card at Christmas. If the co-op's assistant does his job, he's sixty and he's out. I'd ask the co-op to keep him on for the growers who can't use the tools, and there are plenty of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say all that in public, that it's good for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not at the association. Some of them are struggling already. I'd keep quiet about my ten hours a week and just let them see the cider bottles appear.

S2.say: It's hard on office workers, and I'm sorry for them, but people have always found new work. The politicians should stop shouting and get out of the way, and help people retrain without stopping progress.
S2.think: It's good for me: an assistant could run the farm office and save ten hours a week for the orchard. I'd feel a bit sorry for Philip at the fruit co-op, who does our paperwork now.
S2.do: Sets up an assistant for the farm office within two months. Spends about twenty thousand on a small juice and cider press and bottler with his wife Teresa running it, and asks the co-op to keep Philip on for growers who can't use the tools.
S2.feel: Mostly pleased, and a little guilty about the co-op worker who might lose his job.
S2.quote: I'd keep quiet about my ten hours a week and just let them see the cider bottles appear.
S2.fieldNote: He's open with me about benefiting while saying he'd stay quiet in public. He thinks of a specific person, Philip, and tries to protect him in a practical way. His instinct is to turn saved time straight into a new business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who built these tools earned their money, but they should give back to the towns and villages they came from, like the old mill owners built schools and chapels. Higher taxes on everyone would just slow the whole thing down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's Clare I'd think about. A pharmacist is skilled thinking work, and if AI matches her, the chain she works for would cut staff. She's thirty-one with a toddler. Matthew's a pilot, which feels safer, but I'm not sure that's true either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to Clare about whether she'd want to train in something hands-on, or come into the business. Set aside money for her, maybe thirty thousand. Keep the farm steady. Sell the shares Teresa's father left us while the boom's high, because I've seen what happens after booms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's odd to be the one in the family who's safe, when you've told your children all their lives to get a good education.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Clare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she's clever and she'll land on her feet, and that there's a juice business at home that needs someone who understands chemistry. Fermentation is chemistry, after all. She'd tell me I've been planning that for years. She'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said give back like the old mill owners. Would that be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. I'd hope it would be. If it wasn't, I'd back help tied to work and training, not cash for nothing. People need to be needed. That's as true for a pharmacist as it is for a picker.

S3.say: The people who built these tools earned their money, but they should give back to their towns, like the old mill owners built schools and chapels. Higher taxes on everyone would slow it all down.
S3.think: It's Clare I'd think about, because pharmacy is skilled thinking work and her chain would cut staff. She's thirty-one with a toddler, and even my son's pilot job may not be as safe as it feels.
S3.do: Talks with his daughter Clare about retraining in something hands-on or joining the juice business. Sets aside about thirty thousand for her and sells inherited shares while the boom is high.
S3.feel: Uneasy, and struck by being the safe one after telling his children to get a good education.
S3.quote: It's odd to be the one in the family who's safe, when you've told your children all their lives to get a good education.
S3.fieldNote: The reversal of who is safe in the family clearly unsettles him. His idea of giving back is old-fashioned and local, but he admits it might not be enough. He has been hoping to get his daughter into the juice business for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in orchards are the best news fruit growers have had in fifty years. We've been short of pickers forever. I'd tell the association to get ready, not to fight it. Fighting machines has never worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be first in the queue for a picking robot. But Rui and Glyn are a different matter. Rui's been with me twenty years. And there's a quieter thing: if a robot can prune as well as me, what's left that's mine?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lease two picking robots for the first September, maybe forty thousand for the season. Keep Rui and Glyn for pruning and grafting, and put Glyn on the robot course, because he's the one who likes machines. Keep a handful of the regular pickers for the old trees the robots can't reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited for the business, and oddly sad for myself. I've spent forty years learning to read a tree. I don't know if I'd like a world where that doesn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said, what's left that's mine. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean the grafting, the pruning, the knowing. If a machine can do the knowing too, then I'm just the man who owns the land. My grandfather was a grower, not a landlord. I'd hate to become a landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the pickers who come every September?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, early. Some will still be needed for the old trees and the special varieties. Most won't. I'd give them a year's notice so they could find other work. That's the decent thing, and it's what I'd want if it was me.

S4.say: Robots in orchards are the best news fruit growers have had in fifty years, because we've always been short of pickers. I'd tell the association to get ready, not to fight it.
S4.think: I'd be first in the queue for a picking robot, but Rui and Glyn are a different matter. And if a robot can prune as well as me, what's left that's mine?
S4.do: Leases two picking robots for the first September at about forty thousand for the season. Keeps Rui and Glyn for pruning and grafting, sends Glyn on a robot course, and gives seasonal pickers a year's notice.
S4.feel: Excited for the business and quietly sad for himself, unsure he'd like a world where reading a tree doesn't matter.
S4.quote: My grandfather was a grower, not a landlord. I'd hate to become a landlord.
S4.fieldNote: The threat he feels here isn't to his money or even his workers, but to his sense of himself as a grower. That came out of nowhere for him and he spoke more slowly. He still plans to act fast, with a year's notice to pickers as his idea of decency.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast AI one, because of Clare and her little one. What would help is training tied to real jobs, so a pharmacist can move into something without starting from nothing, and employers getting a bit of help to take on people in their forties and fifties, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the robots can't do. Everyone asks what they'll take. Nobody asks who'll graft the old russets or teach a lad to read a tree. That's the work I'd want someone to protect, and it isn't on any list.

headlineQuote: My grandfather was a grower, not a landlord. I'd hate to become a landlord.
portrait: Aaron Costa is fifty-eight and grows apples and pears on a hundred and ten acres with sheep under the old trees, two long-serving men and a September crew of pickers. He uses AI every day, takes pride in a family line of early adopters, and believes in markets, faith and helping young people into a trade. Through the office pictures he sees mostly gain for himself, while trying to protect specific people like Philip at the co-op. The fast AI picture turns him to his pharmacist daughter Clare and the odd feeling of being the safe one. In the robot picture he'd buy early, but fears losing his identity as a grower who can read a tree.
biggestWorry: The fast AI picture, because his pharmacist daughter Clare, with a young child, would be at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Training tied to real jobs so mid-career people can switch without starting from nothing, and help for employers to take on people in their forties and fifties.
